newsitem.title: UK: McCartney tries cartoons, symphonies and painting.
newsitem.headline: McCartney tries cartoons, symphonies and painting.

text.p: Paul McCartney revealed on Tuesday that he is making a cartoon, writing a symphony and trying his hand at painting.
For the Beatle who became one of the 20th century's most famous composers has no plans to retire graciously to the strains of "Will you still need me, will you still feed me when I'm 64."
Clutching Elvis Presley's double bass, he can even do a passable imitation of the King of Rock n'Roll singing "Heartbreak Hotel".
McCartney, who celebrates his 55th birthday next month, marked the release of his first solo album for four years by appearing in a documentary showing how the old ties never die.
Beatle drummer Ringo Starr and producer George Martin joined him for "Flaming Pie" with guest appearances by his photographer wife Linda, now recovering from breast cancer.
The documentary, screened to a packed press conference on Tuesday where McCartney failed to show, showed him presenting the sweeping impressionist canvasses he has done in his new role as an artist.
Linda tracked down and gave him as a present the double bass used on "Heartbreak Hotel," Playing it proudly, he said: "This is a very special piece of wood."
He has also tried his hand at doing most of the voices and singing all the songs for "Tropic Island Hum," the cartoon follow-up to "Rupert and the Frog Song".
McCartney, whose first foray into classical music was the Liverpool Oratorio performed by Kiri te Kanawa, has now turned his hand to a symphonic poem to mark the centenary of his music company.

He decided to make a new solo album after the success of the Beatles Anthology which also produced two previously unheard songs by John Lennon, killed by a crazed gunman outside his New York apartment in 1980.

But McCartney was determined not to spend months sweating away in a studio on an over-produced album lacking all spontaneity: "I wanted to have some fun and not sweat it. You've got to have a laugh because it is just an album."

And for his solo return he opted for a return to Beatle mythology. Lennon, once asked how the Beatles got their name, said: "It came in a vision. A man appeared on a flaming pie and said unto them From this day on, you are Beatles with an A.'"
